The energy gap (band gap) is the gap between the top of the valence band and the bottom of the conduction band. It is the minimum energy a valence electron must gain before it can enter the conduction band and take part in conduction, and this single quantity decides the electrical behaviour of the solid.

1. It classifies the solid. A metal has no band gap at all — its valence and conduction bands overlap — while an insulator has a wide gap. A semiconductor sits between the two, with a gap that is fairly small, of the order of one electron volt or less. At 300 K the chapter gives 1.12 eV for silicon and 0.66 eV for germanium, against 5.47 eV for diamond.

2. It fixes the number of charge carriers. At absolute zero every level up to the topmost band is occupied and the crystal cannot conduct. At a finite temperature an electron gains thermal energy of the order of \(kT\); because the semiconductor gap is small, a few electrons acquire more than the gap energy and cross into the conduction band. Each electron that leaves creates a vacancy — a hole — in the valence band, so the size of the gap controls the density of BOTH kinds of carrier, and through them the conductivity.

3. It makes the conductivity controllable and temperature dependent. Because carriers must be thermally excited across the gap, raising the temperature produces more of them and the conductivity of a semiconductor INCREASES with temperature (Fig. 14.1(b)) — the opposite of a metal, whose conductivity falls. A gap of about an electron volt is small enough for this to happen usefully at room temperature and large enough that the material is not simply a conductor, which is exactly why semiconductors can be tailored for electronic devices.

In short: too wide a gap and the solid is an insulator; no gap and it is a metal; a gap of about 1 eV is what makes a material a semiconductor.

A PENTAVALENT element — one with five valence electrons. The chapter names phosphorus (P), arsenic (As) and antimony (Sb) as the pentavalent impurities used to dope silicon or germanium; any one of them will make germanium n-type.

Why this works: germanium is tetravalent, so each Ge atom forms four covalent bonds with its neighbours. When a pentavalent dopant atom takes the place of a Ge atom in the lattice, four of its five valence electrons form the four bonds and the fifth is left over, very weakly bound to its parent atom. Freeing that fifth electron needs only about 0.01 eV in germanium, so it is available for conduction even at room temperature. Because each such atom DONATES an electron it is called a donor impurity, and the crystal is left with far more free electrons than holes, \(n_{e} \gg n_{h}\) — electrons are the majority carriers and holes the minority carriers, which is what defines an n-type semiconductor.

Note that a trivalent impurity such as boron, aluminium or indium would do the opposite: it would create holes and give a p-type crystal. Note also that the crystal stays electrically NEUTRAL — the extra electrons are supplied by donor atoms that become positively charged ions.

In forward bias the positive terminal of the external supply is joined to the anode (the p-side) and the negative terminal to the cathode (the n-side). The chapter gives two reasons why the carriers then find it easy to cross the junction and the current becomes large.

1. The barrier is lowered and the depletion region narrows. The applied voltage OPPOSES the built-in potential of the junction, so the potential barrier is reduced and the width of the depletion region decreases. The junction therefore offers a low resistance path.

2. The majority carriers are pushed towards the junction and gain extra energy. Electrons in the n-region are driven towards the junction by the applied field, and holes in the p-region are driven towards it from the other side. They arrive with enough extra energy to get over the reduced barrier, cross it in large numbers and contribute to the current.

Because the carriers doing the crossing are the MAJORITY carriers, which are plentiful, the resulting current is large — of the order of a few milliamperes \((10^{-3}\ \text{A})\) for a typical diode. This should be contrasted with reverse bias, where the barrier is raised, the depletion region widens and only the few thermally generated minority carriers get across, giving a leakage current of only a few microamperes \((10^{-6}\ \text{A})\).

[Note: above the knee point the diode behaves practically as a short circuit, so a resistor is used in series with it to limit the current; an excessive current heats the diode and can damage it physically.]

The electrical conductivity of a solid is given by
\(\sigma = n q \mu\)
where \(n\) is the charge carrier density (the number of carriers per unit volume), \(q\) is the charge on the carriers and \(\mu\) is the mobility of the carriers. Since the question fixes the temperature, the factors left are the three on the right-hand side:

1. The carrier density \(n\). In a PURE (intrinsic) semiconductor the two carrier densities are equal, \(n_{e} = n_{h} = n_{i}\), and both electrons and holes contribute to the current. How large \(n_{i}\) is at that temperature is set by the width of the band gap — a narrower gap lets more electrons be thermally excited into the conduction band, each leaving a hole behind.

2. The charge \(q\) on the carriers.

3. The mobility \(\mu\) of the carriers — the measure of how easily a carrier moves through the material under an applied electric field. The chapter lists what mobility itself depends on: the mass of the carrier, whether the material is crystalline or amorphous, the presence of structural defects in the material, and the nature of any impurities present. Electrons and holes do not have the same mobility, the hole mobility being the smaller of the two, so the two carrier types do not contribute equally.

Section 14.2 gives the same list in words, adding the crystal structure of the solid and the types and nature of the defects it contains. (Temperature is also on that list, but it is held fixed by the question — and it matters because it is what sets \(n_{i}\) in the first place.)

Compare the two crystals through \(\sigma = n q \mu\).

At the SAME level of doping the majority-carrier density is the same in both: the n-type crystal has a density \(n_{e}\) of electrons which equals the density \(n_{h}\) of holes in the p-type crystal, because each dopant atom contributes one carrier either way. The magnitude of the charge on a hole is the same as that on an electron. So \(n\) and \(q\) are matched, and the only factor that can differ is the MOBILITY \(\mu\).

The chapter states directly that the mobility of a hole is less than that of an electron, and that the hole current is therefore lesser. The reason it gives is that a hole is not a real particle being transported: physical transportation is of the electrons only. A hole appears to advance only because an electron from a neighbouring bond moves back to fill the vacancy, leaving a new vacancy behind it. This indirect, step-by-step motion means the drift speed associated with holes is less than the drift speed of free electrons in an n-type crystal, so \(\mu_{h} < \mu_{e}\).

With \(n\) and \(q\) equal and \(\mu\) smaller, \(\sigma\) is smaller for the p-type crystal. Hence at the same doping level an n-type semiconductor has the greater conductivity.

[Note: this is also why, when a p-n junction diode is fabricated, the imbalance between the two currents is removed by increasing the doping percentage in the p-region — raising \(n\) there to compensate for the lower \(\mu\), so that the same current flows through both regions.]
